---
title: "Solution: k-Means Clustering"
output: html_document
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

```{r load-packages}
library(tidyverse)
library(cluster)

options(bdat602.source_only = TRUE)
source("courses/bdat-602/_teacher/resources/datasets/simulate_bdat602_data.R")
health_data <- simulate_bdat602(n = 50000, seed = 602)
```

## Task 1: Prepare and scale clustering features

```{r task1-prepare}
clust_data <- health_data |>
  select(age, bmi, income, num_claims, num_chronic_conditions) |>
  drop_na() |>
  scale()

dim(clust_data)
```

```{r task1-check-scale}
apply(clust_data, 2, mean) |> round(4)  # all ≈ 0
apply(clust_data, 2, sd)   |> round(4)  # all ≈ 1
```

## Task 2: Elbow plot — choose k

```{r task2-elbow}
set.seed(602)
wcss <- sapply(1:10, function(k) kmeans(clust_data, centers = k, nstart = 25)$tot.withinss)

tibble(k = 1:10, wcss = wcss) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = k, y = wcss)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2, colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Elbow Method for Optimal k",
       x = "Number of clusters (k)", y = "Within-Cluster Sum of Squares") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r task2-choose-k}
# The elbow typically appears at k = 4 for this dataset:
# WCSS drops steeply from k=1 to k=4, then the reduction flattens.
# k = 4 provides a good balance between interpretability and compactness.
chosen_k <- 4
```

## Task 3: Fit k-means

```{r task3-fit}
set.seed(602)
km <- kmeans(clust_data, centers = chosen_k, nstart = 25)

cat("WCSS:", round(km$tot.withinss, 1), "\n")
cat("Cluster sizes:", km$size, "\n")
```

```{r task3-silhouette}
set.seed(42)
idx <- sample(nrow(clust_data), min(5000, nrow(clust_data)))
sil <- silhouette(km$cluster[idx], dist(clust_data[idx, ]))
cat("Mean silhouette score:", round(mean(sil[, "sil_width"]), 3), "\n")
# A score around 0.15-0.25 is typical for this many features — clusters exist
# but there is natural overlap between similar policyholders.
```

## Task 4: Profile clusters and assign labels

```{r task4-profile}
health_clustered <- health_data |>
  drop_na(age, bmi, income, num_claims, num_chronic_conditions) |>
  mutate(cluster = factor(km$cluster))

cluster_profile <- health_clustered |>
  group_by(cluster) |>
  summarise(
    n          = n(),
    avg_age    = round(mean(age), 1),
    avg_bmi    = round(mean(bmi, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    avg_income = round(mean(income, na.rm = TRUE), 0),
    avg_claims = round(mean(num_claims), 2),
    avg_chronic = round(mean(num_chronic_conditions), 2),
    pct_smoker = round(mean(smoker) * 100, 1)
  )

print(cluster_profile)
```

```{r task4-labels}
# Typical cluster labels (exact values depend on random seed):
# Cluster 1: "Young Healthy Low-Risk"
#   — youngest avg age, lowest BMI, few claims, lowest chronic conditions
# Cluster 2: "Middle-Aged Moderate-Risk"
#   — middle age, moderate income, some claims, occasional smoking
# Cluster 3: "Elderly High-Utilisation"
#   — oldest avg age, highest num_claims and chronic conditions, frequent visits
# Cluster 4: "High-BMI Smoker Segment"
#   — elevated BMI, high smoker rate, more claims than Cluster 1/2
# These labels inform targeted pricing, wellness programme design, and retention strategies.
```
